Before the city learns to argue, it speaks in smaller sounds. A shutter rattles upward. Water runs along a gutter. Somewhere, a bottle settles against another bottle with the soft seriousness of glass. I like walking then, when the pavements are almost empty and the sky has not yet decided what colour to become. There is no destination worth naming. I am simply out, carrying my keys and a little unfinished sleep, watching the familiar streets loosen their ordinary meanings. At that hour, even a traffic light changing for nobody seems less like machinery than a private, patient morning ritual.

The bakery opens first, though open is too public a word. Its door is held back with a flour sack, and the interior glows like a stage before the audience arrives. Inside, a man in a white shirt slides trays into the oven while a radio murmurs the football results. Outside, crates of milk wait beside the newsagent. None of this feels picturesque to the people doing it, nor should it. Their work is heavy, timed, and probably underpaid. Still, seeing it corrects a small arrogance in me: the belief that a day begins when I decide to notice it.

On the corner, an old man tears bread into pieces for sparrows. He does this with both hands, looking down, mouth pursed, as if performing a task requiring precision. The birds know him. They gather before he takes the bag from his coat. When I pass, he says his wife used to buy too much bread on purpose. She has been dead six years, he adds, without being asked. Then he laughs at the birds fighting over a crust. I walk on, unsure whether I have witnessed grief, habit, or a loyalty that no longer needs to distinguish between them.

Farther on, the shops display their previous lives. A phone repair sign has been screwed over the painted letters of a chemist. Above a shuttered cafe, stone cherubs hold a wreath no one looks at. During the day, commerce makes everything seem current. Dawn is less convinced. It lets the layers show. I read dates in cornices and names on doorbells, aware that attention can resemble time travel, though only in the modest sense of noticing that other people were here first. Their ambitions survive as stained brick, bent railings, tiled entrances leading nowhere, and trees growing through small yards.

My phone could guide me home in twelve minutes. It could also rank the nearby coffee, summon a car, and convert this walk into a bright green line. I am grateful for such competence, especially when lost or late. But efficiency has a quiet way of becoming the only question. What is the fastest route? What is worth seeing? What has already been approved by several thousand strangers? Wandering asks poorer questions, which is its usefulness. It permits a street to be merely interesting, a detour to remain unjustified, and time to pass without producing anything except a blue door.

By the river, the light has become silver. A nurse cycles past me in the direction of home, her badge still clipped to her pocket. Two runners move along the embankment with the grave concentration of people keeping a promise. Under a bridge, someone is asleep inside a tent, one hand resting outside it. Dawn does not make the world innocent, and I should not use its beauty to varnish over that fact. It only changes the angle from which I see. Every life nearby is keeping a different time, and morning is not a beginning for everyone at once.

Near the park gate, a woman sits on the lowest step with a book closed over one finger. Her dog watches a squirrel with such stillness that the leash seems irrelevant. We exchange the cautious nod of people who have decided not to become a story in each other’s morning. A moment later, the squirrel leaps, the dog stands, and the book slips to the ground. We look at one another. Then she laughs, and I do too. Nothing follows, which is precisely what makes it pleasant: a tiny, unrepeatable agreement that for three seconds we occupied the same world.

When the sun clears the rooftops, windows catch fire one by one. Buses fill. The man outside the bakery lights a cigarette and studies the street as though it has personally disappointed him. My own day begins assembling its evidence: messages, errands, a conversation I have postponed, the familiar arithmetic of not quite enough time. Nothing has been solved by walking. Yet the worries return to a slightly larger room. They remain real, but they no longer occupy every wall. This may be all perspective means: not a noble explanation, just space around a thought to let you move again.

Walking home, I notice how quickly inattention returns. I step over the same cracked paving stone without seeing it, think about breakfast, and rehearse an answer to an email. This used to disappoint me, as though awareness were a summit from which only weak people descend. Now it seems more like tidying a table. The surface will be covered again by keys, cups, and unfinished work. You clear it not because you expect permanence, but because a little space changes what can happen next. Attention is similar: less a virtue to possess than a courtesy you keep offering the world.

I do not think everyone needs dawn, or a river, or an old man feeding birds. Those are merely the instruments available to me this morning. The practice is smaller and more portable: leave one errand by a different route, look above the shopfronts, let a conversation finish without reaching for your phone. Keep some modest portion of the day unclaimed by improvement. The world will not always reward you. Often it is wet, tedious, or painful, and no amount of noticing makes it otherwise. But sometimes a shutter rises, glass touches glass, and the street breathes before it speaks.
